mappings.note: Leave an ice cube out, observe, and conclude that ice and water are one substance. A conducted observation with an inference drawn, LO-82.

Water on a steel plate: infer where it went, and judge whether the activity alone proves the plate does not leak. LO-82 -- the second part is about the sufficiency of the evidence, which is investigation, not content.
Record the droplets on the tumbler's outside and the questions that arise. Observation recorded during an activity, LO-82.
Predict, then weigh the cold tumbler every five minutes for half an hour. LO-82 for the predict-and-test design, LO-85 because the evidence is a mass measured on a balance.
Fill the shape, flow and spread table for ice, water and vapour. An explicit differentiation of the three states on their properties, LO-80.
Cap versus plate evaporation, then name what was kept the same, what was changed and what was measured. A controlled investigation described in its own terms, LO-82.
Repeat the evaporation activity on a windy or rainy day and record what changes. Varying a condition and re-observing, LO-82.
Build a pot-in-pot cooler, explain how it cools, and test how long produce stays fresh. LO-87 is construct a model from surrounding materials and explain its working, exactly this.

The answer labels the water-cycle diagram -- ocean, lake, river, with arrows for evaporation. LO-86 names the water cycle among its own diagram examples. The stem and answer are mismatched: the stem carries the cloud-in-a-bottle activity.
Which option best describes condensation. Defining a change of state, LO-84; nothing is being sorted, so not LO-81.
Where evaporation matters -- water colours drying, ink from a pen. Applying the process to everyday materials, LO-88. The stem is broken: its two sub-parts have been folded into the option list.
Why air above real grass feels cooler than above plastic grass. The item asks for the cause -- evaporation draws heat -- LO-83.
Name liquids besides water that evaporate. Identifying materials by a shared observable behaviour, LO-79.
Why a fan dries clothes although evaporation needs heat, not cold air. Resolving an apparent contradiction by naming the real cause, LO-83.
Why drain sludge is left in heaps before being carted to a field. Evaporation applied to a real civic practice -- lighter load, safer handling, LO-88.
Spot evaporation in a day's household activities and say how knowing it helps. Applying the learning in day-to-day life, LO-88.
How water appears in nature as a solid -- snow, glaciers, icebergs, hail. Identifying natural forms of one state, LO-79.
Reflect on 'water is our responsibility before it is our right'. A call to use water wisely and keep it clean for the future, LO-89's protect-the-environment register.
How to cool the sun-heated seat of a parked two-wheeler. Using evaporative cooling to solve an everyday problem, LO-88.
Ice and water are two STATES of one substance. Naming the forms a material takes, LO-79.
An ice cube left at room temperature melts. Explaining the change of state, LO-84.
Puddle water becomes vapour and joins the air. Explaining where the water went, LO-84.
Definition of evaporation as liquid to vapour. Naming a change of state, LO-84.
Steam is vapour plus tiny condensed droplets, which is why it is visible. Explaining a phenomenon that is commonly misread, LO-84.
WHY droplets appear on a cold tumbler -- surrounding vapour condenses on the cold surface. The cause is the marked answer, LO-83.
Definition of condensation as vapour to liquid. Naming a change of state, LO-84.
The weighed tumbler gains mass as vapour condenses onto it. The evidence is a measured mass, LO-85, which is this chapter's clearest claim on that outcome.
How ice differs from liquid water in shape. An explicit differentiation of two states by a property, LO-80.
How vapour differs from liquid water in spreading and shape. A differentiation of two states, LO-80.
Solid to liquid is melting. Naming a change of state, LO-84.
Molten wax solidifying as another instance of freezing. Placing a second substance in the same change-of-state class, LO-81.
Greater exposed surface makes water evaporate faster. A factor that governs the rate, LO-83.
Clothes dry faster in sun because higher temperature speeds evaporation. A cause of the observed difference, LO-83.
Humidity is the amount of water vapour in the air. Naming a property of the surrounding air, LO-79.
Why matka water feels colder -- seepage through pores then evaporation, which draws heat. The causal chain is the answer, LO-83.
Dust particles give vapour a surface to condense on. The cause of cloud droplet formation, LO-83.
What the water cycle is -- water circulating between surface and atmosphere. Explaining the process, LO-84; the diagram items get LO-86.
Plasma is not an everyday state of water. Tests the boundary of the three-state classification, LO-81.
The key DIFFERENCE between evaporation and condensation. An explicit differentiation of two processes by direction, LO-80.
Which factor slows evaporation -- high humidity. A factor governing the rate, LO-83.
How to dry clothes fast on a dull day -- use a fan. Applying the evaporation factors to a household problem, LO-88.
Assertion-reason with a FALSE reason: ice floats because it is LESS dense than water, unusually for a solid. Requires differentiating solid from liquid on density, LO-80.
Which listed events are liquid-to-gas changes. Sorting everyday events by the change of state involved, LO-81. The stem retains only the last of the three numbered items.
The wet outside of an iced lemonade glass is condensation from humid air. The cause of an everyday observation, LO-83.
Invisible water in the air at room temperature is water vapour. Naming a state from its observable absence, LO-79.
Droplets on a cool plate held over steam demonstrate condensation. Naming the process shown, LO-84.
Liquid to solid is freezing. Naming a change of state, LO-84.
Which increased factor slows evaporation -- humidity. A factor governing the rate, LO-83.
Compare ice and water on shape and flow. A differentiation of two states by property, LO-80.
Which everyday case is NOT evaporation -- dew, which is condensation. Sorting events by change of state, LO-81.
The pot-in-pot cooler's sand must be kept moist. Maintaining a constructed model so it keeps working, LO-87.
Assertion-reason: vapour rises, cools at height and condenses into cloud. The causal chain is what is marked, LO-83.
Which conditions speed evaporation -- low humidity and high temperature, but not still air. Factors governing the rate, LO-83. The stem retains only the last of the three numbered conditions.
Visible breath on a cold morning is warm moist air condensing. The cause of an everyday observation, LO-83.
The Thirukkural line about even the ocean draining without rain. Reading a text for the water-cycle idea it carries, LO-84.
Sanitizer cools the hands because evaporating alcohol takes heat from the skin. The cause of a sensation, LO-83.
Liquid to gas BELOW the boiling point is evaporation, not boiling. A differentiation of two processes on the condition that separates them, LO-80.
Name the process the water-cycle DIAGRAM shows rising from oceans and rivers. Reading a labelled diagram of a process, LO-86, whose own example is the water cycle.
How the three states differ in ability to flow. A three-way differentiation on one property, LO-80.
The different forms of one substance are its states. Naming the forms a material takes, LO-79.
